title: Action, devotion, knowledge
hookLine: Arjuna's whole journey from collapse to standing, and the three roads to God it teaches
carry: three roads to god: action, devotion, knowledge

lines: SEVEN HUNDRED VERSES LATER, HE STANDS.
cards: Go back to the first morning. Two armies face each other on the field of Kurukshetra. Conches blow.
Arjuna asks Krishna, his charioteer, to drive between the lines so he can see who he's about to fight. He sees teachers, uncles, cousins, old friends. His mouth goes dry.
I won't fight, he says, and he drops his bow and sits down in the chariot. That's chapter one. Seven hundred verses later, the same man stands up.
Today, how he got there, in one go.

teach.b: Krishna doesn't answer with one argument. He answers with three roads, and Hindus have walked all three ever since. One traditional teaching aid splits the eighteen chapters into three sets of six to show them.
The first road is karma yoga, the yoga of action. Chapters one to six: do your work, offer it, and let go of the fruit. You have a right to the action, not to its result.
The second road is bhakti yoga, the yoga of devotion. Chapters seven to twelve: love God. Offer me a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water, with love, Krishna says, and I accept it.

The third road is jnana yoga, the yoga of knowledge. Chapters thirteen to eighteen: know what you really are. The body is a field, and the one who knows the field is your true self; one light shines in every field.
The labels are a teaching aid; all three run through the book. And in chapter eighteen they meet: reflect fully, then choose; come to me for refuge.
Arjuna says, my confusion is gone, and stands. Here's the big Hindu idea under it: there isn't only one way up.
Someone who serves, someone who sings to God, someone who asks hard questions: each is on a real road, and most people walk some of all three.
That's why one Hindu home can hold a grandmother at her altar, a father who calls his work his offering, and a teenager who won't stop asking why.

how: Hindu teachers often speak of three yogas, or paths: karma (action), bhakti (devotion) and jnana (knowledge); some read the Gita's eighteen chapters as three sets of six built around them, and some Hindus recite the whole Gita on Gita Jayanti.

games.q: your grandmother prays at her altar every morning. your dad says his work is his offering. you keep asking why. who's on a real Hindu path?
o: only grandma: real religion is prayer.
all three: devotion, action and knowledge are each a yoga.
only you: asking questions is the only honest way.
games.why: the Gita teaches bhakti, karma and jnana yoga. most people walk some of all three.

practice: Picture Arjuna on the floor of the chariot, then standing. Now try each road for a few breaths. Action: think of one task tomorrow, and offer it before you begin.

Devotion: if you pray, say a name of God you love; if you don't, think of someone you love without asking anything back. Knowledge: ask quietly, who is the one noticing all this? Notice which road felt most like home.

wordCard.voice: Gita, song. The Song of the Blessed One: one conversation, about seven hundred verses, and three roads: action, devotion and knowledge.

orig.note: Sanskrit: bhagavad-gita, the song (gita) of the Blessed One (bhagavan).

carryVoice: Your line: three roads to God: action, devotion, knowledge. Arjuna sat down on the first page and stood up on the last. Tomorrow, the verses that stay.
